Photograph: Sagar Ghosh/Alamy View image in fullscreen Lush countryside in Indore, Madhya Pradesh – the state is home to India’s largest forest area. Photograph: Sagar Ghosh/Alamy This Is India World news The whitewashing of the Green India Mission forest expansion project The flagship environmental initiative has achieved ‘negligible’ results. Why so little progress, and what are the risks as the planet gets hotter? Plus, fusion dance pioneer Usha Jey Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Niha Masih Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.03 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I ndia set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”. Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture. I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk. Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found. 1. Forest cover v forest cover The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced . The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific , pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover. “A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me. The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations. 2. Whose land is it anyway? Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet. Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects. 3. Ground zero The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament. One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%. View image in fullscreen Coalmining has affected forests and other ecosystems in areas such as Madhya Pradesh. Photograph: Sushil Chikane/Alamy 4. The ‘ great’ project Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes. The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore) . The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists. “Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire , arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones. 5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer? For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound. Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy. “We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said. A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said. All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. RaGa, on Delhi’s upmarket Janpath Road, starts serving on 26 August . Surviving summer | What is it like to endure extreme heat in a city pushed beyond its capacity to cope? In a dispatch from Mumbai’s sweltering summer in Equator magazine , Aruna Chandrasekhar provides a dystopian glimpse of a climate-stressed future. Cost of reporting | Uttar Pradesh journalist Abhishek Upadhyay , among the first to report on the theft of donations at Ayodhya’s Ram Mandir Temple, has alleged police harassment and retaliation over his reporting. Guest shelf A recommendation from someone with great taste View image in fullscreen Gathering’s Roly Poly hand-painted jacket. Photograph: Gathering Textiles Diet Sabya (@dietsabya ), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “ Gathering by Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’” Count it A number worth knowing View image in fullscreen Patients in a makeshift care centre in New Delhi during Covid-19 – the PM Cares fund was set up in the early days of the pandemic. Photograph: Money Sharma/AFP/Getty Images Rs 8,452 crore The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of £647m (Rs 8,452 crore) at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in a debate on Times Now , saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters. Vibe check View image in fullscreen Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, centre, with hybrid bharatham dancers in Usha Jey’s video Hide N Seek. Photograph: Youtube For choreographer and director Usha Jey (@usha_jey ), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video, Hide N Seek . Directed by Jey and her longtime partner, Gavin Emishka, the film is a striking visual treat featuring two dance forms in fluid negotiation. Photograph: Stelios Misinas/Reuters Greece Greek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosion Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’ Helena Smith in Athens Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 13.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Greek authorities say they are trying to discover what caused a two-storey apartment block in the heart of ancient Athens to collapse “in a matter of seconds”, killing six people. Emergency teams found the victims, including four American tourists, on Saturday, more than 24 hours after the early morning explosion in the historic Plaka district. The fire service said the bodies of three women and three men had been found, but stopped short of identifying them. A Briton and his Greek wife, 77 and 78, who lived in a flat on the building’s upper floor, were among those killed, the Guardian was told. “The bodies have been taken to the morgue where postmortems will be conducted,” the city’s vice-mayor, Paris Charlaftis, said in a telephone interview from the blast scene. “Our focus now is on the explosion’s cause. What could have happened to bring the building down in a matter of seconds?” Rescuers had deployed thermal cameras and geophones, used to detect deep subsonic frequencies, in the hope of finding survivors. Earth-moving machines and specially trained search dogs were brought in to move and comb mounds of rubble through the night. Before the bodies were pulled from the ruins on Saturday, police put the missing at six, saying four were Americans staying in a short-term rental on the building’s first floor. Two brothers and their wives, all four were due to fly to the US on Friday, just hours after the explosion. View image in fullscreen A rescuer searches the remains of the building. Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty Images “When they failed to turn up for the flight they had checked into only a day earlier, that gave us a further lead,” a source said. “It became clearer that they must have been there when the blast occurred.” The Briton, a talented artist, who lived with his wife on the second floor, was described by Charlaftis as being partially disabled. “He had kinetic issues, and it was thought likely they, too, were in the building [at the time of the blast].” Nestled around the foot of the fifth-century BC Acropolis, Plaka is especially popular with tourists. The picturesque district draws thousands of visitors daily, with many staying overnight in the hotels and short-term rentals in neoclassical houses and small apartment blocks along its alleyways and narrow streets. The mayor of Athens, Haris Doukas, who rushed to 15 Lysikratous, where the mid-20th-century building had once stood, was quick to describe the incident as an “unprecedented disaster”. At least three people were known to have been injured when the explosion occurred at 7.30am, shattering the windows of nearby buildings and scattering debris far and wide. A motorist driving down Lysikratous described how his car was lifted into the air by the sheer force of a blast that some in the neighbourhood likened to an earthquake, others to a bomb. Emergency workers could be seen hastily removing two women on stretchers from a building next door who had been wounded by flying debris. Speculation is rife that a gas leak triggered the collapse but officials said there were many “cogent theories” at play. Fears of the leak emanating from the first-floor short-term rental was among them. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion As part of efforts to address a burgeoning housing crisis, Greece ’s centre-right government has sought to ban short-term rentals in Plaka – clamping down on permits and tightening regulations. On Saturday, as speculation mounted over the cause of the blast, criticism grew over the ability to “properly control” establishments that were often unregulated. “This awful incident will fuel further debate over who inspects short-term rentals that no one who lives in Plaka wants anyway,” said Giorgos Zafeiriou, an architect who heads the local residents’ committee. “Hotels have chambers that regulate them but who inspects and controls Airbnb and serviced apartments that often may not be up to par?” Civil protection crews and emergency disaster management teams have been ordered to remain on site until the cause of the explosion is found, officials said. “It was a huge explosion, so getting to the bottom of it must now be the priority,” added Zafeiriou. “Six people have lost their lives.” Explore more on these topics Greece Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Greece announces social media ban for under-15s, citing anxiety and sleep problems Former Greek PM Tsipras savages ‘celebrity’ ex-finance minister Varoufakis in memoir Greece announces €1.6bn relief package to tackle population decline Wildfire burns through northern suburb of Athens as residents told to evacuate Two wounded in Greece after explosion at home of prison guard official Greek PM seeks ‘reset’ with former far-right activist as migration minister Strasbourg court finds Greece guilty of ‘systematic’ pushback of asylum seekers At least five dead as migrant boat capsizes in Greek waters Thirteen arrested after fireworks from yacht spark forest fire on Greek island Erdoğan hails ‘new era’ of friendship with Greece on historic visit to Athens Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
